# Lab 1: Environments as Code {.unnumbered} The [first lab](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-1-env-as-code.html#lab01) includes two Quarto documents: ::: {.cell} ::: ```{.default} _labs/lab01/ ├── eda-basic.qmd └── model-basic-py.qmd ``` ## Project-oriented workflows Key takeaways: 1. Each project should have an **isolated** package environment that preserves the names and versions. 2. The project's dependencies/requirements should be captured in a way that **makes it exportable/transferable to another machine**.[^renv-venv] 3. Each project should have a **virtual environment** in a **standalone directory** that documents everything the project needs (usually in a GitHub or GitLab repo).[^rstats-wtf-projects] [^rstats-wtf-projects]: Read more in [What They Forgot to Teach You About R: Chapter 3, Project-oriented workflow](https://rstats.wtf/projects) [^renv-venv]: In R, this is [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html). In Python, this is [`venv`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment). ## Virtual environments `venv` and `renv`, "*keep user-level package caches of the actual packages and use symlinks, so only one copy of the package is installed.*" ### `renv` First, read the documentation on [project level management with `renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html) and [using renv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-renv). I’ve summarized the steps below: ```r # create a new R project-local environment install.packages("renv") renv::init() # install packages into the renv-managed environment install.packages(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2")) # snapshot the state of the environment and package versions in # the lock file (renv.lock) renv::snapshot() # to deactivate the environment, restart R or close the session # renv projects are automatically reactivated the time a project # is opened # restore the environment on a new system with renv::restore() ``` To demonstrate how to use `renv`, I've copied the `eda-basic.qmd` file into it's own 'project' folder (`renv-eda-basic`): ```{.default} _labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/ └── eda-basic.qmd ``` Then I ran `renv::init()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::init() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Initiating `renv` in a project root directory will create the `.Rprofile` and `renv.lock` files and a `renv/` folder: ```{.default} _labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/ ├── .Rprofile ├── eda-basic.qmd ├── renv/ ├── renv-eda-basic.Rproj └── renv.lock ``` `renv::init()` will also create `renv-eda-basic.Rproj`, which helps enforce project-oriented workflows (but these are specific to RStudio). To install the packages, we can use `install.packages()` or `pak::pak()` for more flexible installations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("pak") pak::pak(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2")) ``` ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [**Note**]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: #282b2d;'} `renv::install()` will install cached packages if they are available if not, it will install the latest version from CRAN. ::: :::: Create a snapshot (i.e., the current versions of R and any installed packages, along with the R repositories) with `renv::snapshot()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::snapshot() ``` ::: The dependencies are saved in the `renv.lock` file, which should be committed to version control. To make sure the dependencies in the `renv.lock` file have been installed (i.e., after cloning), run: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::restore() ``` ::: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'renv' %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% flowchart TD %% External sources CRAN("CRAN/
GitHub/...") %% Local components SysLib("system
library") ProjLib("project
library") RenvCache("renv
cache") Lockfile("lockfile") %% Subgraph for "your computer" vs "the internet" subgraph Internet ["Internet"] CRAN end subgraph Computer ["Computer"] SysLib ProjLib RenvCache Lockfile end %% Connections with function labels SysLib -->|"init()"| ProjLib CRAN -->|"install()
update()"| RenvCache RenvCache -->|"renv"| ProjLib ProjLib <-->|"status()"| Lockfile ProjLib -->|"snapshot()"| Lockfile Lockfile -->|"restore()"| ProjLib %% styling %% classDef default fill:#F2E6C2,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 style CRAN fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style SysLib fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style RenvCache fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style ProjLib fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Lockfile fill:#485466,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Internet fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#5B8C5A,color:#1B2A41 style Computer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 ``` ### `venv` Read the [documentation on Python virtual environments](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment) and using [venv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-venv). I've summarized the steps below: ```bash # create new Python 3 virtual environment in the '.venv' directory python3 -m venv .venv # activate the environment source .venv/bin/activate # use pip to install packages into your environment python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas # deactivate an environment deactivate # save environment python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt # restoring environment python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Use the **Terminal** to navigate to the `venv-model-basic-py` folder and create the Python virtual environment: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv ``` This will create a `.venv/` folder inside `venv-model-basic-py`. ::: {.cell} ::: ```{.default} _labs/lab01/venv-model-basic-py/ ├── .venv │ ├── bin │ ├── include │ ├── lib │ └── pyvenv.cfg └── model-basic-py.qmd ``` To activate the virtual environment, run the following in the **Terminal**: ```bash source .venv/bin/activate ``` This should change the **Terminal** prompt from: ```bash Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$ ``` to: ```bash (.venv) Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$ ``` Now we can install required Python packages (we include `jupyter` for interactive outputs) ```bash pip install palmerpenguins pandas numpy scikit-learn jupyter ``` To store the installed packages ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'venv' %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% flowchart TD %% External sources PyPI("PyPI/
GitHub/...") %% Local components SysPython("system
Python") VirtEnv("virtual
environment") PipCache("pip
cache") Requirements("requirements.txt") %% Subgraph for "your computer" vs "the internet" subgraph Internet ["Internet"] PyPI end subgraph Computer ["Computer"] SysPython VirtEnv PipCache Requirements end %% Connections with function labels SysPython -->|"python -m venv"| VirtEnv PyPI -->|"pip install
pip upgrade"| PipCache PipCache -->|"pip"| VirtEnv VirtEnv <--->|"pip list
pip show"| Requirements VirtEnv -->|"pip freeze"| Requirements Requirements -->|"pip install -r"| VirtEnv %% Additional workflow arrows VirtEnv -.->|"source activate
deactivate"| VirtEnv %% Styling style PyPI fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style SysPython fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style VirtEnv fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style PipCache fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Requirements fill:#485466,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Internet fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#5B8C5A,color:#1B2A41 style Computer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 ``` #### Rendering with Python To render, use the following in the **Terminal**: ```bash quarto preview model-basic-py.qmd --no-browser --no-watch-inputs ``` To tell Quarto to use the virtual environment, we can place the following in the `model-basic-py.qmd` file: ```yaml execute: python: .venv/bin/python ``` Or we can set the Python interpreter with the **Terminal**:[^venv-win] ```bash quarto use python .venv/bin/python3 ``` [^venv-win]: On Windows try `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` If you're working inside **RStudio or Posit Workbench**, consider letting `reticulate` manage the Python environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(reticulate) use_virtualenv("myenv", required = TRUE) virtualenv_install( envname = "myenv", packages = c("palmerpenguins", "pandas", "numpy", "scikit-learn", "jupyter")) ``` ::: This ensures RStudio uses a known-good Python environment. Now, if we open the `model-basic-py.qmd` file in RStudio and click the **Render** button in the toolbar we should see the rendered output.
